root.note: Wiktionary derives Portuguese esquerda from Basque ezkerra (the form with the article), from Proto-Basque *ezkeR ‘left hand’; for Galician it also allows a common Paleo-Hispanic source behind both.

history: Most Portuguese words are Latin, but ‘left’ is not. The Latin word, sinister, carried bad luck, and people avoided it. In Iberia the gap was filled from Basque, the old language of the Pyrenees, where ezker means left. The word passed through Old Spanish exquerdo into Portuguese esquerdo, and pushed out the older Portuguese word that came from sinister. Spanish izquierda has the same Basque origin. You will use the word every day: vire à esquerda, ‘turn left’, a mão esquerda, ‘the left hand’. In politics a esquerda is ‘the left’. And on a Portuguese doorbell, esq. after a floor number means the flat on the left: 2.º esq.
historyEinfach: Esquerda means ‘left’. Vire à esquerda means ‘turn left’. The word is not Latin. It probably comes from Basque, an old language in the north of Spain and the south of France: in Basque, ezker means ‘left’. Spanish izquierda comes from the same word.

elsewhere.text: One of the few Basque words in everyday Portuguese.
The Latin left came into English as a word for something evil.
